title: The bounded loop
point: Four independent bounds, on steps, tokens, wall clock and progress, each catch a pathology the others miss, and a bounded stop returns a typed reason.
definition: A bounded loop runs choose, act and observe under four independent limits: a step ceiling, a token budget, a wall-clock limit and a no-progress detector. Hitting any bound ends the run with a typed termination reason, not a crash.

objective.text: Given a run budget, configure four independent termination bounds and predict which fires first for three given traces.

misconceptions.claim: A step ceiling alone is enough to bound a loop.
misconceptions.correction: Ten steps can still read a 200,000-token document ten times or wait minutes on a slow API. Token and wall-clock bounds catch failures that a step count never sees.

misconceptions.claim: Hitting a bound is an error, so it should raise an exception.
misconceptions.correction: A bounded stop is expected behaviour. The run returns a typed termination reason, such as a step-limit reason, so the caller can degrade, retry or explain.

l1: The step ceiling catches oscillation, where a planner flip-flops between two actions. The token budget catches a loop that keeps re-reading a huge observation.
The wall-clock limit catches slow dependencies. The no-progress detector catches identical repeated calls and steps that add no new information.
The bounds are independent because each catches a failure the others miss. When one fires, the run ends with a typed termination reason rather than a crash.
l2: Take a budget of 12 steps, 60,000 tokens, 90 seconds, and a stop after three consecutive identical calls.
Trace A alternates between two tools, each step costing 1,000 tokens and 2 seconds. No two consecutive calls match, so the step ceiling fires at step 12, after only 12,000 tokens and 24 seconds.
Trace B re-reads a 15,000-token document every step. After four steps it has spent 60,000 tokens, and a fifth would project 75,000, so the token budget stops it before step 5.
Trace C calls a search API that takes 40 seconds per call. After two calls 80 seconds have passed, so the wall-clock limit fires during step 3 at the 90-second mark.
l3: Setting the step ceiling trades false stops against wasted spend. If 99 per cent of successful runs finish within 9 steps, a ceiling of 12 leaves sensible headroom.
Compare a ceiling of 30. An oscillating run at 1,000 tokens and 2 seconds per step would then burn 18 extra steps: 18,000 tokens and 36 seconds for nothing.
Defend the number from the distribution of successful runs, and review it when that distribution shifts.
